foodDescription: Native flat oysters from Mali Ston Bay, an hour up the coast, where fresh springs mix with the sea. They have been farmed there for centuries. Eaten raw with lemon, best from late winter to spring.
Risotto cooked with cuttlefish or squid and colored black by their ink. Found on nearly every menu on the coast. It stains your teeth for an hour, which everyone accepts.
Several kinds of fish stewed slowly with tomato, wine, and vinegar, and usually served with polenta to soak up the sauce. A fisherman’s dish, made with whatever came in.
Dubrovnik’s old winter dish: cabbage and other greens cooked for hours with smoked ham, dried meats, and sausage. Families still make it in winter, especially for feast days.
Pasta tossed in a rich sauce of beef slow-cooked with tomato, wine, and spices. “Dirty” because the meat sauce messes up the pasta. A Dubrovnik feast-day dish, now on some restaurant menus.

foodEnglishName: Meat or octopus under the bell
foodDescription: Lamb, veal, or octopus roasted with potatoes under an iron lid covered in embers. It takes hours, so many restaurants ask you to order a day ahead.
A baked custard with a caramel top, like a crème caramel, flavored with rozalin, a rose liqueur that gives the dessert its name. Dubrovnik’s signature dessert.
An unusual cake from Ston made with macaroni pasta, walnuts, chocolate, cinnamon, and sugar, baked in pastry. Said to date back to the days of the republic.
In Dubrovnik, arancini are not Sicilian rice balls but strips of bitter orange peel boiled in syrup and rolled in sugar. Often made at home and served with coffee or a glass of brandy.
A firm, sweet paste of quince, cut into squares and dusted with sugar. Traditionally made in autumn and kept through winter, especially for Christmas.
A white wine from Konavle, the valley south of the city. The republic’s nobles drank it, and growers revived the grape after it nearly disappeared.
Croatia’s best-known red grape, grown on the steep, sunny slopes of the Pelješac peninsula north of Dubrovnik. The wines from Dingač, a stretch of its coast, are the most prized.
A sweet wine made from dried grapes, drunk in small glasses with dessert or offered to guests. Not related to Italian prosecco, though the similar names led to a long dispute over EU labels.
